keyVerseText: And it came to pass, when midday was past, and they prophesied until the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, that there was neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded. offering: Heb. ascending that regarded: Heb. attention
rootMeaning: The root of קֶשֶׁב (qesheb) is קָשַׁב (qâshab), which fundamentally means to attend, listen carefully, or give heed. This root conveys an active inclination of the ears and mind toward something, emphasizing deliberate and focused attention rather than passive hearing. Thus, the literal sense of qesheb goes beyond mere hearing to imply a diligent and intentional readiness to receive and respond.
usageInScripture: The word qesheb appears four times in Scripture, consistently connected to the idea of attentiveness or diligent hearing. It is translated primarily as "diligently" in two instances, while also rendered as "nor any that regarded" and "nor hearing" in other contexts, showing a spectrum from active listening to the absence of such attentiveness. This range highlights the importance of focused attention as both a spiritual posture and a sign of life, as seen in its use to describe a living deity and human responsiveness.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding qesheb enriches our grasp of biblical faith as one that calls for more than superficial hearing; it demands heartfelt attentiveness and earnest hearkening to God's voice. This word underscores the relational nature of faith, where God invites His people to incline their ears and minds toward Him with diligence. Such attentiveness reveals the vitality of spiritual life and obedience, reflecting a living connection with God. It also challenges believers to cultivate a posture of listening that is active and responsive, essential for growth in Christ and faithful discipleship.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Kings 18:29, the phrase "nor any that regarded" (Hebrew "attention") uses qesheb to highlight the absence of genuine attentiveness among the prophets. The verse depicts a moment of spiritual silence and unresponsiveness, where no one inclined their ears or hearts to hear God's voice. This underscores the critical role of qesheb as not just hearing but truly paying heed, reminding readers that spiritual vitality involves active engagement with God's word and presence.
